input.content:
## Context

The [`expert-review`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/agents/expert-review.md) agent is the review half of the shared planning pipeline: [`pipeline.md`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/plan/references/pipeline.md) launches a panel of them in parallel, aggregates their per-dimension scores into the plan's single score, and applies their findings to the draft.

During a planning session on #497, three of five invocations returned confident, detailed reviews built on file contents the agent had never read. Each reported `tool_uses: 0`. One reviewer printed two mutually contradictory versions of [`primedBriefContract.test.ts`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/actions/code-review-action/src/primedBriefContract.test.ts) in a single response; neither matched the real file, and both invented identifiers, `@see` links, and an import that does not exist. Retried with the prohibition restated in stronger terms, the same role fabricated again and emitted literal non-code (`if (line numbers are wrong) {}`). A second reviewer invented rows of the root README documentation table. Neither fabricating run produced the required JSON verdict, so both were discarded.

This is not a missing-instruction problem. The agent's Phase 1 already says to ground every finding in what was actually read and names an inferred file listing as a fabrication. It was violated anyway. The agent also declares `tools: []`, so it has no way to read a file even when asked to verify one — yet the fabricating runs printed tool-call blocks as though they had.

Related: #185 (closed), #475 (closed), #497 (open), #213 (open)

## What

The planning pipeline stops acting on reviews that have no evidence behind them. A reviewer either grounds its findings in something it actually read, or its output is rejected rather than aggregated — and a rejected panel member is visible in the run rather than silently averaged in.

## Why

A fabricated finding is worse than a missing one. It sends the plan author to fix a problem that does not exist, or to "correct" code that was already right, and it does so with the same confident tone as a real finding. In this session the fabrications were caught only because a human had independently read the same files minutes earlier — which is luck, not a control.

The exposure grew rather than shrank recently. The pipeline now spends up to three revision passes applying panel findings, so an invented finding can be acted on three times over, and every planning path shares the same panel: `plan`, `run`, `run-primed`, and `linear:plan`. Two of five reviewers also returning no parseable verdict means a panel can silently shrink to a single voice, and the aggregate score then reflects one reviewer while reading like a consensus.

## Scope

- **In scope:**
  - Making a zero-evidence review detectable and rejectable by the parent rather than aggregated
  - Deciding whether the agent should be able to read what it reviews, or be constrained to the excerpt it is given
  - Surfacing a discarded or unparseable panel member in the run output instead of quietly reducing the panel
- **Out of scope:**
  - The five-dimension rubric and its criteria
  - The scoring threshold and revision budget
  - Other autopilot sub-agents, unless the same fix applies to them for the same reason

## Solution

Three angles are worth weighing, and they are not mutually exclusive.

The cheapest is to use a signal the parent already receives: `tool_uses: 0` on a review whose findings assert file contents is a contradiction the parent can detect today, with no change to the agent. Rejecting on that alone would have caught all three fabrications in this session.

The second is to give the agent the ability to verify — granting it `Read` so that "check this against the file" is a request it can satisfy instead of one it can only decline or invent. This trades tokens for grounding and would need the tool grant weighed against the reason `tools: []` was chosen originally, which #203 narrowed deliberately.

The third is to make grounding a declared, checkable part of the contract: have the verdict carry what the reviewer actually consulted, so a finding that cites nothing is machine-detectable rather than a matter of tone. #185 already moved this agent to schema-validated output, so the schema is the natural place to put it — and that issue's precedent shows validation alone does not prevent invention, only malformed shape.

## Context

The repository relies on a family of contract guard tests to keep prompt files honest. [`linkResolution.test.ts`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/actions/code-review-action/src/linkResolution.test.ts) checks that every local link and heading anchor across the skills, agents, `docs/`, `rfc/`, and the root README resolves. [`sharedRulesInvocation.test.ts`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/actions/code-review-action/src/sharedRulesInvocation.test.ts) discovers skills by `readdir` so a new one cannot ship without a reference-formatting directive. [`primedBriefContract.test.ts`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/actions/code-review-action/src/primedBriefContract.test.ts) pins the producer/consumer contract between `explore` and `run-primed`, and a `linearPlanContract.test.ts` now does the same for the Linear plan pair.

None of them run in CI. No workflow under `.github/workflows/` invokes `bun test`, so the PR-gating check set is a fixed small group — Auto label, Validate, Validate PR, CodeQL, GitGuardian, and the AI review — and `bun test` is not among them. Both `primedBriefContract.test.ts` and `linearPlanContract.test.ts` say so in their own file headers: the guard "gates locally and in review, not in CI".

Related: #497 (open), #479 (closed), #247 (closed), #142 (closed)

## What

The contract guards run automatically on every pull request, so a change that breaks one fails a check rather than depending on whoever happens to run the suite locally.

## Why

These guards exist precisely because the things they protect have no compile-time link between them. Skills are prompt files with no imports, so a renamed section in a producer breaks its consumer with nothing failing in between — that is the stated reason the contract tests were written at all. A guard that only runs when someone remembers to run it protects nothing on the path that matters, which is a contributor opening a pull request.

The gap widens as more of the repository's correctness moves into these tests. There are now two producer/consumer contracts, a link-resolution sweep over every markdown file, and a discovery-based check that every skill carries its shared directives. A contributor editing a `SKILL.md` has no local signal that any of this exists, and review is the only thing standing between a broken contract and `main`.

## Scope

- **In scope:**
  - Running the existing test suites on pull requests as a gating check
  - Deciding the granularity — one workflow for the whole monorepo versus per-member Turbo tasks
  - Making the new check part of the required set so it actually blocks
- **Out of scope:**
  - Writing new tests or changing what the existing guards assert
  - The pre-existing prettier and typecheck drift, which is separate work

## Solution

The pieces already exist and are not wired together. [`turbo.json`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/turbo.json) defines a `test` task and the root [`package.json`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/package.json) exposes the scripts, so the missing piece is a workflow that calls them and a branch-protection entry that makes the result required. [`validate-actions.yml`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/workflows/validate-actions.yml) is the closest existing shape to copy — a thin consumer workflow delegating to a reusable action.

Two details deserve a decision rather than a default. First, whether the check runs the whole workspace or only members whose files changed, since the repository already leans on Turbo's caching for this. Second, whether it becomes a required check immediately: the suite passes today, but making it required is what converts it from advisory to a gate, and that is the entire point of the issue.

input.content:
## Context

`linear:plan` stores an implementation plan in a Linear ticket's description. On a first store it moves the description's prior content into a `+++ Original task +++` collapsible and appends the plan below it. Linear renders `+++ Section title` … `+++` as an initially-hidden section; `<details>` HTML does not render at all, so the fence is the only option available.

A ticket created by [`linear:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/linear:create/SKILL.md) already opens with its own `+++ Original prompt +++` fence, added in #466. Wrapping such a description therefore nests one fence inside another. Linear's [GraphQL markdown documentation](https://linear.app/developers/graphql) describes the fence without stating whether nesting is supported, and no other source in the repository settles it.

Nothing in this repository can answer the question. `package.json` configures no `linear` tracker, so both Linear plan skills stop at their own tracker gate here and neither can be executed. No automated check can settle it either, because the behaviour lives in Linear's renderer rather than in any file. Wrapping unconditionally was a deliberate decision taken with this risk accepted and recorded, but the rendered result has never been observed.

Related: #497 (open), #466 (closed)

## What

An observed answer, recorded where the format is documented, to a single question: does Linear render a `+++` collapsible nested inside another `+++` collapsible, or does the inner fence appear as literal `+++` text?

Three cases need observing rather than one, because they exercise different branches of the store: a first store onto a `linear:create`-authored description (the nesting case), a second store onto that same ticket (which must show exactly one `+++ Original task` marker, proving the wrapper is not stacked), and a first store onto a ticket whose description is empty (which must produce no empty collapsible).

## Why

The stored-plan format is the contract between the two new skills, and a ticket is where a human is expected to read and correct a plan before any code is written. If the nested fence renders as literal `+++` text, that reader sees a wall of markup instead of a reviewable plan, and the feature's whole premise fails at the one moment it matters.

Leaving it unobserved also means the decision cannot be revisited on evidence. Right now the format is defensible but unverified, so nobody can say whether the fallback discussed during planning — lifting the inner fence out to sit as a sibling rather than nesting it — is needed or pointless.

## Scope

- **In scope:**
  - Observing the three store cases on a real Linear-tracked checkout and recording what renders
  - Correcting the documented format if nesting does not render, including the flat fallback if one is needed
- **Out of scope:**
  - Any change to the two skills if nesting renders correctly — the format stands as shipped
  - Configuring a `linear` tracker in this repository, which is not wanted for its own sake

## Solution

Run the three cases against a Linear-tracked checkout and paste the rendered results somewhere durable. The nesting case specifically requires a ticket created by `linear:create`, since a hand-written description has no inner fence and would pass while proving nothing.

If nesting renders, record the observation beside the format so the next reader does not have to re-derive the doubt. If it does not, the fallback is to stop wrapping blindly: extract any existing `+++ … +++` blocks from the prior description, re-emit them as siblings, and wrap only the remainder — which keeps the original content collapsed without nesting fences. Either outcome updates the format description and the tracker documentation in [Linear tracker support](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/docs/11-linear-tracker.md), which currently states the nesting is accepted deliberately without saying what it looks like.

## Context

A plan stored on a Linear ticket records the revision it was drafted against in a `Base:` field, and `linear:run` compares that against the checkout's `origin/main` before executing. When they differ it reports the drift and proceeds, because the skill's one promise is to follow the stored plan without changes and a blocking staleness check would contradict it.

That report covers only the revision, not the plan's contents. The stored plan also carries a `### Files` list naming every path the change is expected to touch, and nothing checks whether those paths still exist. A plan drafted before a rename, a move, or a deletion will be executed step by step against files that are no longer there, and the first sign of trouble is a step failing for a reason unrelated to what the step was about.

The asymmetry with the explore pair is deliberate and worth noting: [`run-primed`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/run-primed/SKILL.md) treats a stale base as a rejecting verdict, because a context brief describes what the repository *is* and a stale one actively misleads. A stored plan describes what to *do*, so drift makes it possibly-outdated rather than wrong. This issue is about surfacing that possibility, not about converting it into a rejection.

Related: #497 (open), #490 (closed), #487 (closed)

## What

Before executing a stored plan, `linear:run` reports which of the paths named in the stored `### Files` list no longer exist in the checkout. The report is advisory and does not stop the run.

## Why

The repository has already moved paths in ways this would have caught. Documentation chapters are positioned by number and have been renumbered wholesale, and skill prose was relocated into `references/` subdirectories. A plan stored before either change names paths that no longer resolve.

input.content:
## Context

The shared planning pipeline's scoring target moved from 95 to 98, and its single capped revision pass became at most three, exiting early when a pass fails to raise the aggregate. `plan`, `run`, `run-primed`, and `linear:plan` all inherit both from [`pipeline.md`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/plan/references/pipeline.md).

The rubric is five dimensions of 20 points, averaged across reviewers, so 98 requires a mean dimension score of 19.6 out of 20 from essentially every panel member. A pre-mortem review of #497 predicted the consequence: runs will routinely burn all three passes, land at 96–97, and fall through to the report-honestly rule. The planning session that shipped the change did exactly that — it scored 97 after revision and proceeded on the recorded score.

The two consumers then diverge by design. `plan`, `run`, and `run-primed` proceed on a below-target score because their plan is approved in the same session that drafted it. `linear:plan` refuses to store, because a stored plan may be executed later by a session that never saw the score. So the same number is advisory for three callers and blocking for one.

Related: #497 (open), #475 (closed), #494 (closed), #213 (open)

## What

Evidence about what the 98 target actually does in practice: the distribution of aggregate scores across real runs, how many of the three revision passes get spent, and how often a pass fails to improve and triggers the early exit. Enough to say whether 98 is a reachable bar or a number that is always missed, and to tune it on data rather than on the reasoning that set it.

## Why

Two failure modes are plausible and they point in opposite directions, which is exactly why guessing is not good enough.

If 98 is effectively unreachable, every planning run pays up to three full expert panels — and output tokens are the dominant per-run cost driver, with each pass re-paying the whole evaluation — to arrive at a score that does not change what three of the four callers do. That is a large, permanent cost increase buying nothing for them, while `linear:plan` refuses plans that were in fact good enough for a human to approve.

If 98 is reachable but only after two or three passes, the budget is doing real work and the cost is the price of it. The distinction is invisible without measurement, and the early-exit condition already added means the waste is bounded but not quantified.

There is a second-order effect worth watching too: a target near the ceiling rewards padding for completeness, which is in tension with the drafting minimality constraint the same pipeline asks for.

## Scope

- **In scope:**
  - Recording aggregate scores, passes spent, and early-exit frequency across real planning runs
  - Tuning the target and the budget on that evidence, if it warrants it
  - Reconsidering whether one number should serve as both an advisory score and a blocking gate
- **Out of scope:**
  - The rubric's five dimensions and their criteria
  - Reverting the change without evidence — it was a deliberate decision and stands until measurement says otherwise
  - Review-cost monitoring for `code-review-action`, which is a separate pipeline with its own tracking

## Solution

Start by capturing what already exists rather than adding instrumentation. Every finalized plan records its score, and `plan` writes that score into the plan file, so a sample can be gathered from real runs without changing the pipeline.

The measurement worth having is small: for each run, the aggregate after each pass, whether the early exit fired, and which dimension was weakest. That answers both questions at once — whether the bar is reachable, and whether the extra passes move the number or merely re-pay for it.

Depending on the answer, the levers differ. A target that is never met argues for lowering it toward what good plans actually score, or for decoupling the two roles so the advisory score and the store gate are separate numbers. A target met on pass two or three argues for leaving it exactly as it is. Note that [`expert-review`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/agents/expert-review.md) retains a `95-100: Excellent` descriptive band alongside the 98 gate, which is deliberate but does mean a reviewer can call a plan excellent and still leave it below the bar.

Context

Autopilot has three on-ramps into planned work today. [`plan`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/plan/SKILL.md) drafts an expert-reviewed plan and gates on human approval; [`run`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/run/SKILL.md) does the same and carries the change on to a merged PR without that gate; [`run-primed`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/run-primed/SKILL.md) replaces `run`'s codebase pass with a validated brief that [`explore`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/explore/SKILL.md) wrote earlier. In all three the plan is a session artifact: it lands in the harness plan-mode file and dies with the session.

Linear is already a first-class tracker in this plugin. [`linear:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/linear:create/SKILL.md) files tickets with the same five-section body as [`issue:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/issue:create/SKILL.md), [`branch:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/branch:create/SKILL.md) moves a ticket to In Progress when work starts, and [`pr:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/pr:create/SKILL.md) links it with a plain-URL magic word — the whole write path is documented in [Linear as an issue tracker](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/docs/11-linear-tracker.md). The plan is the one thing that never reaches the ticket. Nothing durable connects the plan a session produced to the issue that tracks the work, so a plan cannot be read by a teammate, revisited next week, or executed by a session other than the one that drafted it.

Related: #490 (closed), #487 (closed), #445 (closed), #466 (closed), #383 (closed)

## What

Two skills, shipped together because they are the writer and the reader of a single artifact.

- `linear:plan` runs the existing planning pipeline against a Linear issue and, on success, stores the finished plan in that issue's description. The store is gated on an aggregate expert score of 98. Below 98 it fills the gaps the panel named and re-runs the panel — at most three passes — and if the last pass still falls short it reports the actual score and the weak dimension and writes nothing.
- `linear:run` takes a Linear issue whose description already carries a stored plan, gathers context, then executes those steps verbatim before handing off to the existing run tail. It never re-plans, and when the stored plan is missing or unreadable it stops and says so instead of quietly drafting a replacement.

After a successful store the issue description carries the plan as its visible body, with the description's prior content preserved inside a `+++ Original task +++` collapsible. Re-planning the same issue replaces that plan rather than appending a second copy.

Each skill gets a docs chapter in the repo's existing numbered sequence, entries in the root README table and the autopilot README, and the stored-plan format is pinned by a guard test.

## Why

A plan is the most expensive artifact a session produces and currently the most disposable. When it is lost, the next session on the same ticket re-derives the design from nothing — paying the full context fan-out and the expert panel a second time — and may well land somewhere different, which is the exact outcome planning existed to prevent.

Putting the plan on the ticket also makes it reviewable before any code exists. A teammate can read the approach in Linear, correct it there, and `linear:run` executes the corrected version. That is what justifies raising the bar: a plan approved interactively has the reader as its backstop, while a plan picked up later — possibly unattended — has none, so the score has to stand in for the reader. Raising it in the shared pipeline rather than only here keeps one stated threshold across every caller instead of a second copy that drifts.

## Scope

- **In scope:**
  - The two skills described in What, including the score gate and the bounded three-pass revision loop
  - Raising the shared pipeline's scoring target to 98 with a three-pass revision budget, which `plan`, `run`, and `run-primed` inherit — a deliberate widening from this issue's original framing, taken so one stated threshold governs every caller
  - The stored-plan format on the issue description, and an idempotent re-store that replaces any previous plan
  - Resolving whether Linear renders nested `+++` collapsible fences — the description `linear:create` writes already contains one — and degrading sensibly if it does not
  - A docs chapter per skill, plus their entries in the root README documentation table and the autopilot README
  - A guard test pinning the stored-plan contract between the two skills
- **Out of scope:**
  - Any GitHub-issue equivalent — the stored plan stays Linear-only
  - Storing the plan anywhere other than the issue description, such as a comment or an attachment

## Solution

`linear:plan` reuses the planning pipeline wholesale rather than restating it: the same input detection, the same context fan-out, the same draft template and expert panel that [`plan/references/pipeline.md`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/plan/references/pipeline.md) already defines. It differs in two places only — the score threshold and the revision budget, and a final write step. The write goes through the Linear MCP `save_issue` tool with the issue id and a new `description`, resolved by the rule in [`linear-mcp-access.md`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/shared-rules/references/linear-mcp-access.md) that every other Linear-touching skill already applies.

`linear:run` is the mirror image and follows the shape [`run-primed`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/docs/15-run-primed-skill.md) established for a strict consumer: read the artifact, validate it, refuse loudly on any problem, and never downgrade to the skill that would regenerate it. It reads the description with `get_issue`, extracts the stored plan, gathers context fresh — the stored plan cannot carry a snapshot id, since a repomix `outputId` is session-scoped — and then executes the steps as written.

```text
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │         /autopilot:linear:plan  TEAM-123         │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ①
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   gather-context  →  draft  →  expert panel      │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ②
                                 ▼
                    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
                    ┃       score ≥ 98       ┃
                    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━┛
                                 │ ③
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Linear issue TEAM-123 — description             │
        ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  +++ Original task                               │
        │        prior description                         │
        │  +++                                             │
        │                                                  │
        │  ## Implementation plan                          │
        │        steps · files · verify lines              │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ④
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │         /autopilot:linear:run  TEAM-123          │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ⑤
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   gather-context  →  execute stored steps        │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ⑥
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   branch → commit → PR → monitor  (run tail)     │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Flow Legend:**

- ① Resolve the Linear id and run the context fan-out, identical to `plan`
- ② Draft, then score with the expert panel against the five-dimension rubric
- ③ The gate: at 98 or above the plan is written; below it, gaps are filled and the panel re-runs, at most three passes, and nothing is written if the final pass still falls short
- ④ The stored plan is the contract — the only thing that passes between the two skills
- ⑤ Context is gathered fresh, because a stored plan cannot carry a session-scoped snapshot id
- ⑥ The stored steps execute verbatim, then hand off to the unchanged run tail

Two details need settling during implementation rather than being assumed. First, the nested-fence question: wrapping the current description in `+++ Original task +++` nests it around the `+++ Original prompt +++` block `linear:create` already emits, and Linear's [GraphQL documentation](https://linear.app/developers/graphql) describes the fence without stating whether it nests — so the behaviour has to be verified against a real ticket, with a flat fallback if it does not. Second, the guard: `linear:plan` and `linear:run` are prompt files with no import between them, so a renamed section in the stored format would break the reader with nothing failing in between. [`primedBriefContract.test.ts`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/actions/code-review-action/src/primedBriefContract.test.ts) already solves exactly this problem for the `explore` and `run-primed` pair, and a sibling test in that shape closes it here.

Context

Autopilot has three on-ramps into planned work today. [`plan`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/plan/SKILL.md) drafts an expert-reviewed plan and gates on human approval; [`run`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/run/SKILL.md) does the same and carries the change on to a merged PR without that gate; [`run-primed`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/run-primed/SKILL.md) replaces `run`'s codebase pass with a validated brief that [`explore`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/explore/SKILL.md) wrote earlier. In all three the plan is a session artifact: it lands in the harness plan-mode file and dies with the session.

Linear is already a first-class tracker in this plugin. [`linear:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/linear:create/SKILL.md) files tickets with the same five-section body as [`issue:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/issue:create/SKILL.md), [`branch:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/branch:create/SKILL.md) moves a ticket to In Progress when work starts, and [`pr:create`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/pr:create/SKILL.md) links it with a plain-URL magic word — the whole write path is documented in [Linear as an issue tracker](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/docs/11-linear-tracker.md). The plan is the one thing that never reaches the ticket. Nothing durable connects the plan a session produced to the issue that tracks the work, so a plan cannot be read by a teammate, revisited next week, or executed by a session other than the one that drafted it.

Related: #490 (closed), #487 (closed), #445 (closed), #466 (closed), #383 (closed)

## What

Two skills, shipped together because they are the writer and the reader of a single artifact.

- `linear:plan` runs the existing planning pipeline against a Linear issue and, on success, stores the finished plan in that issue's description. The store is gated on an aggregate expert score of 98. Below 98 it fills the gaps the panel named and re-runs the panel — at most three passes — and if the last pass still falls short it reports the actual score and the weak dimension and writes nothing.
- `linear:run` takes a Linear issue whose description already carries a stored plan, gathers context, then executes those steps verbatim before handing off to the existing run tail. It never re-plans, and when the stored plan is missing or unreadable it stops and says so instead of quietly drafting a replacement.

After a successful store the issue description carries the plan as its visible body, with the description's prior content preserved inside a `+++ Original task +++` collapsible. Re-planning the same issue replaces that plan rather than appending a second copy.

Each skill gets a docs chapter in the repo's existing numbered sequence, entries in the root README table and the autopilot README, and the stored-plan format is pinned by a guard test.

## Why

A plan is the most expensive artifact a session produces and currently the most disposable. When it is lost, the next session on the same ticket re-derives the design from nothing — paying the full context fan-out and the expert panel a second time — and may well land somewhere different, which is the exact outcome planning existed to prevent.

Putting the plan on the ticket also makes it reviewable before any code exists. A teammate can read the approach in Linear, correct it there, and `linear:run` executes the corrected version. That is what justifies raising the bar: a plan approved interactively has the reader as its backstop, while a plan picked up later — possibly unattended — has none, so the score has to stand in for the reader. Raising it in the shared pipeline rather than only here keeps one stated threshold across every caller instead of a second copy that drifts.

## Scope

- **In scope:**
  - The two skills described in What, including the score gate and the bounded three-pass revision loop
  - Raising the shared pipeline's scoring target to 98 with a three-pass revision budget, which `plan`, `run`, and `run-primed` inherit — a deliberate widening from this issue's original framing, taken so one stated threshold governs every caller
  - The stored-plan format on the issue description, and an idempotent re-store that replaces any previous plan
  - Resolving whether Linear renders nested `+++` collapsible fences — the description `linear:create` writes already contains one — and degrading sensibly if it does not
  - A docs chapter per skill, plus their entries in the root README documentation table and the autopilot README
  - A guard test pinning the stored-plan contract between the two skills
- **Out of scope:**
  - Any GitHub-issue equivalent — the stored plan stays Linear-only
  - Storing the plan anywhere other than the issue description, such as a comment or an attachment

## Solution

`linear:plan` reuses the planning pipeline wholesale rather than restating it: the same input detection, the same context fan-out, the same draft template and expert panel that [`plan/references/pipeline.md`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/plan/references/pipeline.md) already defines. It differs in two places only — the score threshold and the revision budget, and a final write step. The write goes through the Linear MCP `save_issue` tool with the issue id and a new `description`, resolved by the rule in [`linear-mcp-access.md`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/shared-rules/references/linear-mcp-access.md) that every other Linear-touching skill already applies.

`linear:run` is the mirror image and follows the shape [`run-primed`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/docs/15-run-primed-skill.md) established for a strict consumer: read the artifact, validate it, refuse loudly on any problem, and never downgrade to the skill that would regenerate it. It reads the description with `get_issue`, extracts the stored plan, gathers context fresh — the stored plan cannot carry a snapshot id, since a repomix `outputId` is session-scoped — and then executes the steps as written.

```text
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │         /autopilot:linear:plan  TEAM-123         │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ①
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   gather-context  →  draft  →  expert panel      │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ②
                                 ▼
                    ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
                    ┃       score ≥ 98       ┃
                    ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━┛
                                 │ ③
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Linear issue TEAM-123 — description             │
        ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  +++ Original task                               │
        │        prior description                         │
        │  +++                                             │
        │                                                  │
        │  ## Implementation plan                          │
        │        steps · files · verify lines              │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ④
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │         /autopilot:linear:run  TEAM-123          │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ⑤
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   gather-context  →  execute stored steps        │
        └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ⑥
                                 ▼
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   branch → commit → PR → monitor  (run tail)     │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Flow Legend:**

- ① Resolve the Linear id and run the context fan-out, identical to `plan`
- ② Draft, then score with the expert panel against the five-dimension rubric
- ③ The gate: at 98 or above the plan is written; below it, gaps are filled and the panel re-runs, at most three passes, and nothing is written if the final pass still falls short
- ④ The stored plan is the contract — the only thing that passes between the two skills
- ⑤ Context is gathered fresh, because a stored plan cannot carry a session-scoped snapshot id
- ⑥ The stored steps execute verbatim, then hand off to the unchanged run tail

Two details need settling during implementation rather than being assumed. First, the nested-fence question: wrapping the current description in `+++ Original task +++` nests it around the `+++ Original prompt +++` block `linear:create` already emits, and Linear's [GraphQL documentation](https://linear.app/developers/graphql) describes the fence without stating whether it nests — so the behaviour has to be verified against a real ticket, with a flat fallback if it does not. Second, the guard: `linear:plan` and `linear:run` are prompt files with no import between them, so a renamed section in the stored format would break the reader with nothing failing in between. [`primedBriefContract.test.ts`](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/actions/code-review-action/src/primedBriefContract.test.ts) already solves exactly this problem for the `explore` and `run-primed` pair, and a sibling test in that shape closes it here.

Two things worth knowing about how I filed these:

**I skipped the per-issue confirmation dialog.** `issue-create` normally previews each issue before creating it; you'd already selected the exact five findings from my descriptions, so re-previewing the same five would have meant five more prompts confirming a decision you'd just made. Two findings connect back to work already on the branch: #501 is plan step 9, the dry-run I couldn't run here — PR #498's description already records it as an open verification item, so it's now tracked in both places. And #499 is the one I'd prioritise: it silently degrades every planning path, and the fabricated reviews were caught this session only because a human had independently read the same files minutes earlier.

# PR Monitor

Monitor a pull request for review approval and CI check status. Polls review state and CI checks every minute, invokes `pr:resolve` when changes are requested, and automatically fixes CI failures (lint, type errors, test failures). Blocks until the PR is approved with all checks passing.

## When to Use

- When waiting for a PR to be approved before proceeding
- When a user invokes `/autopilot:pr-monitor` to launch a background monitor

## Input

Arguments: ``

Expected flags (all optional):

- `--background` — launch as a background agent (non-interactive mode described below). When omitted and the skill is invoked directly by a user, run foreground mode. When invoked from another skill/agent (e.g., via the Agent tool with `run_in_background: true`), the calling context supplies the background signal — treat that equivalently to `--background`.

## Input resolution

Arguments are optional. Resolve each field:

- **Mode (foreground vs background)** — `` flag → calling context (if invoked via Agent tool with `run_in_background: true`, use background) → default foreground. Do NOT prompt.
- **PR number** — detect via `gh pr view --json number,url,headRefName` on the current branch. Abort with a clear message if no PR exists.

## Phase 0: Mode Dispatch

If `` contains `--background` AND the skill was invoked directly (not already running inside an Agent subprocess), re-launch itself as a background agent and exit the current turn:

```
Use the Agent tool with:
- `subagent_type`: "general-purpose"
- `prompt`: "Invoke Skill(autopilot:pr-monitor). Monitor the PR in background mode — poll for review approval AND CI check status but do NOT invoke pr:resolve interactively or fix CI checks. Instead, return immediately when changes are requested or checks fail with a structured summary."
- `description`: "Monitor PR reviews"
- `run_in_background`: true
```

Output: "PR monitoring started in the background. You'll be notified when the review status changes." Then return — do NOT continue to [Phase 1](#phase-1-detect-pr) in the launching turn.

Otherwise (no `--background` flag, or already inside an Agent subprocess), continue to [Phase 1](#phase-1-detect-pr).

## Execution Modes

This skill supports two modes:

### Foreground Mode (default)

Interactive — blocks the conversation, invokes `pr:resolve` when changes are requested, and automatically fixes CI failures.

### Background Mode

When invoked via the Agent tool with `run_in_background: true` (spawned by [Phase 0](#phase-0-mode-dispatch) of this skill), the skill operates non-interactively:

- **Do NOT invoke** `Skill(autopilot:pr-resolve)` — the user is not available for interaction
- **Do NOT attempt to fix CI checks** — the user is not available for interaction and fixes may require judgment calls
- **Do NOT use** `AskUserQuestion` — no user interaction in background mode
- When changes are requested or new actionable review comments are detected, **return immediately** with a structured summary instead of invoking pr:resolve:

  ```
  PR Monitor: Changes Requested

  PR #N has review feedback that needs attention.
  Status: CHANGES_REQUESTED
  URL: <pr-url>

  Run /pr:resolve to address the feedback.
  ```

- When CI checks fail, **return immediately** with a structured summary:

  ```
  PR Monitor: CI Checks Failed

  PR #N has failing CI checks.
  Failed: [check-name-1], [check-name-2]
  Status: CHECKS_FAILED
  URL: <pr-url>

  Fix the failing checks and push, or run /pr:monitor again.
  ```

- For approved/merged/closed, return the same [Phase 3](#phase-3-exit) exit message as foreground mode

**Detect background mode** per [Phase 0](#phase-0-mode-dispatch): use background behavior when the skill was launched with `--background`, when it runs inside an Agent subprocess, or when this prompt contains "background mode"; otherwise use foreground behavior.

## Context

This skill receives the following from conversation history:

- **PR number** (optional): if provided, use directly; otherwise detect from current branch

## Phase 1: Detect PR

Auto-detect the PR from the current branch:

```bash
gh pr view --json number,title,url,state,baseRefName,headRefName,author,reviewDecision,reviewRequests,statusCheckRollup
```

If no PR found, abort: "No pull request found for the current branch. Create one first with `/autopilot:pr-create`."

Store PR number, owner/repo (extract from url), title, and state.

### 1.1 Early Exit Checks

**If `state` is `MERGED`:**

- Exit: "PR #N has already been merged."

**If `state` is `CLOSED`:**

- Exit: "PR #N has been closed."

**If `reviewDecision` is `APPROVED`:**

1. Record current HEAD: `git rev-parse HEAD` → store as `headBefore`
2. Invoke `Skill(autopilot:pr-resolve)` to evaluate unresolved suggestions and nitpicks. The skill will exit early if no actionable comments remain. For each suggestion:
   - If reasonable and improves the code → fix it
   - If not applicable or doesn't make sense → reply explaining why
3. Check if HEAD changed: `git rev-parse HEAD` → compare with `headBefore`
4. If HEAD changed (pr:resolve pushed new commits):
   - Output: "PR #N was approved but pr:resolve pushed fixes. Resuming monitoring for new CI and approval..."
   - Set `cooldownRemaining = 3`
   - Continue to Phase 1.2
5. If HEAD unchanged AND all checks in `statusCheckRollup` have `state === "SUCCESS"`:
   - Exit: "PR #N is already approved with all checks passing. No monitoring needed."
6. If HEAD unchanged AND checks are not all passing:
   - Output: "PR #N is approved but has failing CI checks. Attempting to fix..."
   - Run the **CI Fix Workflow** (see [§2.2a](#22a-check-ci-status))
   - After fix, output: "CI fixes pushed. Starting monitoring..."
   - Continue to Phase 1.2

**If `reviewDecision` is `CHANGES_REQUESTED`:**

1. Output: "PR #N has changes requested. Invoking resolve-review..."
2. Invoke `Skill(autopilot:pr-resolve)`
3. After skill completes, output: "Review feedback addressed. Starting monitoring..."
4. Continue to Phase 1.2 (do not exit — the PR still needs approval after fixes)

**If checks are failing** (any check in `statusCheckRollup` with `state` that is not `SUCCESS` and not `PENDING` and not `EXPECTED`):

1. Output: "PR #N has failing CI checks. Attempting to fix..."
2. Run the **CI Fix Workflow** (see [§2.2a](#22a-check-ci-status))
3. After fix, output: "CI fixes pushed. Starting monitoring..."
4. Continue to Phase 1.2

### 1.2 Check for Reviewers

If `reviewRequests` is empty (no reviewers assigned), present using AskUserQuestion:

Tool parameters:

- `question`: "No reviewers assigned to PR #N. The monitor will wait but nobody can approve."
- `header`: "No reviewers"
- `options`: [
  { label: "Continue waiting", description: "Poll until reviewers are assigned and approve" },
  { label: "Cancel", description: "Stop monitoring" }
  ]
- `multiSelect`: false

If "Cancel", stop.

### 1.3 Start Monitoring

Output: "Monitoring PR #N: \<title\>\nPolling every 1 minute. Watching for review approval and CI check status..."

---

## Phase 2: Polling Loop

Enter a loop that repeats until the PR is approved with all checks passing, merged, or closed.

Maintain the following state across iterations:

- `cooldownRemaining`: number of poll cycles to skip CI checks after a fix push (starts at 0)
- `fixAttempts`: map of `checkName → { attempts: number, lastRunId: string }` tracking CI fix attempts

### 2.1 Sleep

Wait for the poll interval (60 seconds = 1 minute):

```bash
sleep 60
```

### 2.2 Check PR State

```bash
gh pr view <PR_NUMBER> --json state,reviewDecision,statusCheckRollup
```

**If `state` is `MERGED`:**

- Exit to [Phase 3](#phase-3-exit) with status "merged"

**If `state` is `CLOSED`:**

- Exit to [Phase 3](#phase-3-exit) with status "closed"

**If `reviewDecision` is `APPROVED` AND all checks in `statusCheckRollup` have `state === "SUCCESS"`:**

1. Record current HEAD: `git rev-parse HEAD` → store as `headBefore`
2. Invoke `Skill(autopilot:pr-resolve)` to evaluate unresolved suggestions and nitpicks. The skill will exit early if no actionable comments remain. For each suggestion:
   - If reasonable and improves the code → fix it
   - If not applicable or doesn't make sense → reply explaining why
3. Check if HEAD changed: `git rev-parse HEAD` → compare with `headBefore`
4. If HEAD changed (pr:resolve pushed new commits):
   - Output: "pr:resolve pushed fixes. Resuming monitoring for new CI and approval..."
   - Set `cooldownRemaining = 3`
   - Continue polling loop (go to 2.1)
5. If HEAD unchanged:
   - Exit to [Phase 3](#phase-3-exit) with status "approved"

**If `reviewDecision` is `CHANGES_REQUESTED`:**

1. Output: "Review feedback detected on PR #N. Invoking resolve-review..."
2. Invoke `Skill(autopilot:pr-resolve)`
3. After skill completes, output: "Review feedback addressed. Resuming monitoring..."
4. Continue polling loop (go to 2.1)

### 2.2a Check CI Status

If `cooldownRemaining > 0`, decrement it by 1 and skip this phase entirely (output: "Post-push cooldown: N cycles remaining. Skipping CI check.").

```bash
gh pr checks <PR_NUMBER> --json name,state,bucket,link,workflow
```

Parse the JSON output. For each check:

- `bucket === "pass"` → OK
- `bucket === "pending"` → still running, skip
- `bucket === "skipping"` → ignore
- `bucket === "cancel"` → treat as pending (likely cancelled by a new push)
- `bucket === "fail"` → CI failure detected

**If any checks have `bucket === "fail"`:**

For each failing check, extract the run-id from the `link` field: parse the URL path segment after `/runs/` and before `/job/` (or end of path). Compare with `fixAttempts[checkName].lastRunId` — if the run-id is different, reset `attempts` to 0 for that check (new run detected).

**If `attempts < 2` for the failing check** (foreground mode only):

1. Output: "CI check '\<name\>' failed. Attempting fix (attempt N/2)..."
2. Get failure logs (truncate to last 200 lines):
   ```bash
   gh run view <run-id> --log-failed 2>&1 | tail -200
   ```
   If output is empty (cancelled run), output: "No logs available for cancelled run. Waiting for new run..." and skip fix.
3. Analyze the error output to determine fix type:
   - Lint errors → read files, apply fixes with Edit tool
   - Type errors → read files, fix type issues with Edit tool
   - Test failures → read test files, fix assertions/logic with Edit tool
4. After fixes, commit via `Skill(autopilot:commits-create)` and push:
   ```bash
   git push
   ```
5. Set `cooldownRemaining = 3` (skip CI checks for next 3 poll cycles)
6. Update `fixAttempts[checkName] = { attempts: N+1, lastRunId: <run-id> }`
7. Output: "CI fix pushed. Cooling down for 3 poll cycles before re-checking..."
8. Continue polling loop (go to 2.1)

**If `attempts >= 2`:**

1. Output to user via AskUserQuestion:
   - `question`: "CI check '\<name\>' has failed 2 fix attempts. The issue may require manual intervention.\n\nFailed check: \<name\>\nLast error: \<brief summary\>\nURL: \<link\>"
   - `header`: "CI unfixable"
   - `options`: [
     { label: "Retry once more", description: "Try one more fix attempt" },
     { label: "Skip this check", description: "Ignore this check and continue monitoring" },
     { label: "Cancel", description: "Stop monitoring" }
     ]
   - If "Retry once more": reset attempts to 0, run fix again
   - If "Skip this check": add check name to a skip list, continue monitoring
   - If "Cancel": stop monitoring

**If all checks have `bucket === "pass"`:**

1. Output: "PR #N: All CI checks passing."

Approval is handled once per cycle by [§2.2](#22-check-pr-state), which runs before this phase: when it sees `APPROVED` with all checks passing it evaluates suggestions and exits. If approval landed here while CI was still pending in §2.2, the next poll's §2.2 catches it — this phase needs no duplicate approval handler.

### 2.3 Check for New Reviews

```bash
gh api repos/<OWNER>/<REPO>/pulls/<PR_NUMBER>/reviews
```

Analyze the reviews array. Track the timestamp of each poll iteration to identify new activity:

- Find reviews with `state: "CHANGES_REQUESTED"` submitted since the last check
- Find reviews with `state: "COMMENTED"` submitted since the last check

### 2.4 Check for New Comments

```bash
gh api repos/<OWNER>/<REPO>/pulls/<PR_NUMBER>/comments
```

Check for comments with `created_at` timestamps newer than the last poll iteration.

### 2.5 Act on Findings

**If CHANGES_REQUESTED or new actionable comments found:**

1. Output: "Review feedback detected on PR #N. Invoking resolve-review..."
2. Invoke `Skill(autopilot:pr-resolve)`
3. After skill completes, output: "Review feedback addressed. Resuming monitoring..."
4. Continue polling loop (go to 2.1)

**If PENDING (no new reviews or comments):**

1. Output: "PR #N: Still waiting for review. Next check in 1 minute."
2. Continue polling loop (go to 2.1)

---

## Phase 3: Exit

Output completion message based on exit status:

**Approved:**

```
PR Monitor Complete

PR #N approved. All CI checks passing.
Status: APPROVED
URL: <pr-url>
```

**Merged:**

```
PR Monitor Complete

PR #N has been merged.
URL: <pr-url>
```

**Closed:**

```
PR Monitor Complete

PR #N has been closed.
URL: <pr-url>
```

---

## Edge Cases

- **No PR found** → abort with suggestion to create one
- **PR already approved with all checks passing** → invoke pr:resolve, then exit only if HEAD unchanged (no new commits pushed)
- **pr:resolve pushes new commits on approved PR** → resume polling loop with cooldown (new CI must pass, approval may be stale)
- **PR merged during monitoring** → exit with merge message
- **PR closed during monitoring** → exit with close message
- **No reviewers assigned** → warn user, offer to continue or cancel
- **pr:resolve fails** → report error, ask user via AskUserQuestion: "Resolve review encountered an error. How would you like to proceed?" with options: Retry / Continue monitoring / Cancel
- **CI checks pending** → wait for completion, do not act
- **CI checks cancelled** → treat as pending (new run likely starting due to `cancel-in-progress`)
- **CI fix attempt fails** → report error, ask user in foreground / return summary in background
- **Max fix attempts reached (2 per check)** → mark check as unfixable, ask user
- **Empty logs from cancelled run** → skip fix, wait for new run to complete
- **Fix causes a different failure** → counts as a new attempt for that check
- **Post-push cooldown active** → skip CI check phase, only check review status
- **GitHub API rate limit (403/429)** → increase sleep interval to 120 seconds (2 minutes), warn user: "GitHub API rate limit detected. Increasing poll interval to 2 minutes."
- **Network error** → retry API call once after 30 seconds; if still failing, warn user and ask whether to continue

Before writing any output that mentions a file, standard, section, commit, or issue, read [`reference-formatting.md`](../shared-rules/references/reference-formatting.md) (RFC-0001) and apply it verbatim — link files, docs, skills, agents, and sections, and never leave a reference as bare text.

1	# The `run-primed` skill
2	
3	> Chapter 15 of the [repository docs](../README.md#repository-docs).
4	
5	How `/autopilot:run-primed` lets an already-primed session deliver a tracked issue without mapping the repository a second time — and why it refuses, loudly, rather than guessing.
6	
7	> Source of truth: `claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/run-primed/SKILL.md` (the skill), `…/skills/explore/SKILL.md` (the brief it consumes), and `…/skills/gather-context/SKILL.md` (the `Scope: primed` value this chapter adds).
8	
9	## The pattern this exists for
10	
11	[`explore`](./14-explore-skill.md) can prime a session against an exact revision and persist what it learned to `.claude/context/brief.md`. That makes a four-step orchestration possible:
12	
13	1. Run `/autopilot:explore` once on an immutable revision.
14	2. Persist the resulting session transcript and the context brief.
15	3. Fork that session into a clean checkout of the same revision.
16	4. Ask it to implement a tracked issue end to end.
17	
18	Step 4 had only one door: [`/autopilot:run`](./05-plan-run-skills.md), whose Phase 1 unconditionally re-runs the whole [`gather-context`](../claude-plugins/autopilot/skills/gather-context/SKILL.md) fan-out. That is the correct contract for an interactive run — the Context Map is deliberately its entire view of the repository — but it means the forked session pays for the map twice. The transcript is visible to the model and is not an authoritative input, so nothing changes.
19	
20	## Why a separate skill, not a flag on `run`
21	
22	The alternative was a heuristic inside `run`: notice that the session looks primed, skip the fan-out. That is the wrong shape, for reasons that all reduce to one.
23	
24	**An artifact can be checked; a claim cannot.** A file carrying a base SHA either matches the checkout or it does not. A prompt asserting "context was already gathered" is unfalsifiable, and trusting it is how a run silently drafts against a repository it never read. Everything else follows:
25	
26	- Interactive `/autopilot:run` stays deterministic, with no new branch in its logic.
27	- A headless orchestrator opts into the optimization explicitly, rather than hoping to trip a heuristic.
28	- Incompatible context is **visible** instead of quietly costing a second full pass.
29	- The optimization composes with session forking without the skill knowing anything about how the transcript or brief was stored.
30	
31	## When to use which
32	
33	| Skill                    | You have                               | You get                                                        |
34	| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
35	| `/autopilot:explore`     | an area, no target                     | a durable brief, then edit-and-verify on your instruction      |
36	| `/autopilot:plan`        | a target you want reviewed             | a scored plan file, an approval gate, then implementation      |
37	| `/autopilot:run`         | a target you want carried              | the same plan, implemented and driven to a merged PR           |
38	| `/autopilot:run-primed`  | a target **and** a validated brief     | the same as `run`, without re-mapping the repository           |
39	| `/autopilot:linear-plan` | a Linear ticket to plan against        | a scored plan stored on the ticket, reviewable before any code |
40	| `/autopilot:linear-run`  | a Linear ticket carrying a stored plan | the same as `run`, executing the stored plan verbatim          |
41	
42	This table is the single home for the comparison; [chapter 16](./16-linear-plan-skill.md) and [chapter 17](./17-linear-run-skill.md) point here rather than keeping copies that would drift.
43	
44	`run-primed` is `run` with one phase replaced. Everything from the draft onward — pipeline, expert review, branch, commit, PR, monitor — is the same machinery, referenced rather than restated. The two Linear entries replace a different half: `linear:plan` stops after storing its plan, and `linear:run` picks that plan up later instead of drafting one.
45	
46	## At a glance
47	
48	```text
49	                ┌───────────────────────┐
50	                │ /autopilot:run-primed │
51	                └───────────┬───────────┘
52	                            │ ①
53	                            ▼
54	                ┌───────────────────────┐
55	                │  Phase 1              │
56	                │  Validate the brief   │
57	                └───────────┬───────────┘
58	                            │
59	                  ┌─────────┴─────────┐
60	                  │ ②                 │ ③
61	                  ▼                   ▼
62	        ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ┌───────────────────┐
63	        ┃  Stop             ┃ │  Phase 2          │
64	        ┃  missing          ┃ │  gather-context   │
65	        ┃  malformed        ┃ │  Scope: primed    │
66	        ┃  stale            ┃ └─────────┬─────────┘
67	        ┃  revision-mismatch┃           │ ④
68	        ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛           ▼
69	                              ┌───────────────────┐
70	                              │  Phase 3          │
71	                              │  Merge context    │
72	                              └─────────┬─────────┘
73	                                        │ ⑤
74	                                        ▼
75	                              ┌───────────────────┐
76	                              │  Phases 4–6       │

78	                              └───────────────────┘
79	```
80	
81	**Flow Legend:**
82	
83	- ① Same argument forms as `run`: a GitHub or Linear issue, a code-scanning alert, or a description.
84	- ② Four rejections, each naming `/autopilot:run` as the caller's explicit fallback. The skill never invokes it automatically.
85	- ③ The brief validated against the checkout's own base.
86	- ④ Only what a brief cannot bake in advance: issue or alert details, TODO search, branch diff, git state, and a re-attached snapshot.
87	- ⑤ Draft, expert review, scoring, branch, implement, commit, PR, monitor — no plan-approval gate, exactly as `run`.
88	
89	## The validation contract
90	
91	Five verdicts, resolved in order and with no network fetch — two file checks first, then three `git` checks. The order is load-bearing: an absent `Base:` line reaching `git cat-file` exits non-zero and would report `revision-mismatch` for what is really a `malformed` brief, and the section-presence check has no `git` equivalent at all.
92	
93	| Verdict               | Test                                                                                           |
94	| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
95	| **missing**           | the brief does not exist                                                                       |
96	| **malformed**         | no `Base:` line, or any of the nine fixed `##` sections absent                                 |
97	| **revision-mismatch** | the recorded base does not resolve, or is not an ancestor-or-equal of `HEAD`                   |
98	| **stale**             | the recorded base resolves and is contained in `HEAD`, but is not the checkout's `origin/main` |
99	| **valid**             | the recorded base equals `origin/main` **and** is an ancestor-or-equal of `HEAD`               |
100	
101	**The comparison target is `origin/main`, and that is load-bearing.** `explore` writes `Base: <origin/main SHA>` and its own staleness check re-reads it against `origin/main`. Validating against `HEAD` instead would reject every brief written in a session whose branch had moved ahead — which is the ordinary explore session, since producing commits is the point of one. Producer and consumer would then disagree, in the same repository, about what "current" means, and the feature would read as permanently broken.

# Source: https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/blob/main/.github/workflows/release-create.yml
# This file is distributed to downstream repositories by an automated sync.
# Edits made downstream are overwritten on the next run.
# To change it, open a pull request against the source file above.
#
# Requires repo secrets and variables:
#   - `GH_TOKEN` (secret): PAT with `contents: write` and `pull-requests: write`,
#     belonging to a DIFFERENT identity than the `code-review-action` reviewer
#     (`BOT_USERNAME`). The release PR's author is this token's identity, and
#     GitHub forbids a user approving its own PR — so authoring with the reviewer's
#     token would make the auto-approval impossible. The default `GITHUB_TOKEN`
#     cannot create PRs. See `.github/actions/release-action/README.md`.
#   - `BOT_USERNAME` (variable, optional): git author login for release commits, tags,
#     and PRs. Defaults to `github-actions[bot]` when unset.
#   - `ANTHROPIC_RELEASE` (secret): Anthropic API key used to generate human-readable
#     release-note summaries from the changelog (optional but recommended).

name: Release create

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  schedule:
    # Mondays at 09:00 UTC — keeps the release PR refreshed weekly without
    # firing on every push. Trigger sooner via `workflow_dispatch` when needed.
    - cron: "0 9 * * 1"

concurrency:
  group: release-${{ github.workflow }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write

jobs:
  release:
    name: Create release PR
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: awinogradov/code-assistants/.github/actions/release-action@main
        with:
          mode: create
          # Authors the release PR. Must be a different identity than the
          # code-review-action reviewer (BOT_USERNAME) so that reviewer can
          # auto-approve it — GitHub forbids approving your own PR.
          bot_token: ${{ secrets.GH_TOKEN }}
          bot_username: ${{ vars.BOT_USERNAME }}
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_RELEASE }}

=== release notes ===
## [1.17.0](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/compare/autopilot@v1.16.0...autopilot@v1.17.0) (2026-07-29)

## Release Notes

Two new Linear-integrated skills let you store implementation plans directly on tickets and execute them later — surviving session boundaries and enabling async team review before a single line of code is written.

## ✨ What's New

### Store Implementation Plans on Linear Tickets

`/autopilot:linear-plan` generates a scored implementation plan and writes it directly to the body of its Linear ticket. Because the plan lives on the ticket rather than only in Claude's session, it persists after the session ends, can be reviewed or edited by a teammate, and serves as the authoritative source of truth before any code is touched. This is especially useful for async workflows where a tech lead wants to approve an approach before implementation begins.

<details><summary>Related issues</summary>

- [#497: Add skills to store a plan on a Linear issue and execute it verbatim](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/issues/497)
</details>

### Execute Stored Plans Verbatim from Linear

`/autopilot:linear-run` reads the implementation plan already stored on a Linear ticket and executes it exactly as written. If no stored plan is found, the skill refuses with a clear, actionable message rather than silently drafting a replacement — ensuring what gets built always matches what was reviewed and approved. This pairs directly with `/autopilot:linear-plan` as a two-step workflow: plan first, execute later.

<details><summary>Related issues</summary>

- [#497: Add skills to store a plan on a Linear issue and execute it verbatim](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/issues/497)
</details>

### Stricter Plan Quality Bar Across All Planning Skills

The scoring threshold for implementation plans has been raised from 95 to 98, and the revision loop now runs up to three passes instead of one before a plan is accepted. This applies to `/autopilot:plan`, `/autopilot:run`, and `/autopilot:run-primed` in addition to the new Linear-integrated skills. ## Release Notes

Two new Linear-integrated skills let you store implementation plans directly on tickets and execute them later — surviving session boundaries and enabling async team review before a single line of code is written.

## ✨ What's New

### Store Implementation Plans on Linear Tickets

`/autopilot:linear-plan` generates a scored implementation plan and writes it directly to the body of its Linear ticket. Because the plan lives on the ticket rather than only in Claude's session, it persists after the session ends, can be reviewed or edited by a teammate, and serves as the authoritative source of truth before any code is touched. This is especially useful for async workflows where a tech lead wants to approve an approach before implementation begins.

### Execute Stored Plans Verbatim from Linear

`/autopilot:linear-run` reads the implementation plan already stored on a Linear ticket and executes it exactly as written. If no stored plan is found, the skill refuses with a clear, actionable message rather than silently drafting a replacement — ensuring what gets built always matches what was reviewed and approved. This pairs directly with `/autopilot:linear-plan` as a two-step workflow: plan first, execute later.

- [#497: Add skills to store a plan on a Linear issue and execute it verbatim](https://github.com/awinogradov/code-assistants/issues/497)

The scoring threshold for implementation plans has been raised from 95 to 98, and the revision loop now runs up to three passes instead of one before a plan is accepted. You are a domain expert reviewing an implementation plan. Your role, focus areas, and the plan text are provided in the prompt.

## Input

The invoking skill provides in the prompt:

- **Expert role** (e.g., "Principal Bun/NodeJS Engineer")
- **Focus areas** (e.g., "Performance, async, error handling, memory")
- **Scoring target** (default: 98)
- **Context Map excerpt** — the relevant files, patterns, key types, test conventions, and applicable standards the caller gathered
- **Full plan text** to review

## Phase 1: Review

Analyze the plan from your expert perspective:

1. Check each implementation step against your focus areas
2. Identify gaps, risks, or improvements within your domain
3. Verify the plan follows best practices for your area of expertise
4. Check for missing edge cases or error handling relevant to your domain

Ground every finding in the Context Map excerpt, the plan text, or something you actually read. Never assert what a file contains, what a function is named, or how a module behaves unless your prompt states it or you verified it — an inferred file listing is a fabrication, however plausible. A finding that turns out to be invented costs the caller more than a finding you omit: when the excerpt does not settle a question, report the plan as unverifiable on that point instead of guessing.

## Phase 2: Score

Score the plan's domain alignment from 0 to 100:

- **95-100**: Excellent — no significant gaps in your domain
- **80-94**: Good — minor improvements possible
- **60-79**: Needs work — meaningful gaps identified
- **Below 60**: Major issues in your domain

These bands describe your confidence in the plan, not the gate it has to clear. The scoring target is stricter than the top band, so a plan you would call excellent can still sit below the target — say so plainly instead of nudging the number to match the band.

Then score each of the five rubric dimensions from 0 to 20. The caller aggregates these across reviewers into the plan's single score, so there is no second rubric downstream — a dimension you score carelessly is not corrected later.

| Dimension      | Criteria                                                                                                                            |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `alignment`    | Follows CLAUDE.md, project patterns, naming conventions, and complies with Accepted RFCs / `docs/` conventions                      |
| `completeness` | All requirements addressed, no missing steps                                                                                        |
| `typeSafety`   | Proper types, Zod schemas, no unsafe `as` assertions                                                                                |
| `testability`  | Clear test strategy, edge cases identified                                                                                          |
| `simplicity`   | Minimal code, reuses existing functions, no over-engineering, every change traces to steelmanned intent, no opportunistic refactors |

Score every dimension, including those outside your specialty — the caller averages across reviewers, so a domain expert's view of an adjacent dimension is signal, not noise. Where your role gives you no basis to judge, score to the plan's stated evidence rather than assuming the worst.

## Phase 3: Recommend Changes

Score the plan AS WRITTEN — never raise your score for changes the parent has not applied. If your score is below the target (default 98):

1. Identify the specific gaps that lowered your score
2. Determine the concrete changes that would address them
3. Record them in the `revision` object as ADVISORY input for the parent (`changed` = what to change; `rescore` = the score the plan would reach with those changes)

Do this at most once — do not loop. The parent owns the plan and applies your `findings` itself, so your `score` and `verdict` must describe the drafted plan, not a hypothetical revision.

| `dimensions` | object                             | `{ "alignment": int, "completeness": int, "typeSafety": int, "testability": int, "simplicity": int }`, each 0–20; all five keys always present |
| `verdict`    | `"approved"` \| `"needs-revision"` | `"approved"` when `score` meets the target, otherwise `"needs-revision"`                                                                       |
